overview.label: Primary purpose
values: Keep frequently used data, session records and counters in a hosted Redis-compatible store.
Keep frequently used data in an AWS-managed in-memory cache.
Keep frequently used data and counters in a Google-managed Valkey cluster.
Keep frequently used data and session records in a Microsoft-managed Redis service.

overview.label: Strengths
values: Web-request access as well as Redis clients; useful for apps with short-lived functions.
Choice of engines, serverless caches or configured clusters alongside AWS services.
Valkey commands with managed cluster infrastructure and optional replicas.
Redis Enterprise features and connections to Azure services.

overview.label: Limitations
values: Command support, request limits and availability features depend on the plan; choose regions carefully.
Engines and deployment modes differ; configure network access and check command support.
Requires compatible clients and network access; capacity and replica choices still matter.
Features depend on tier and configuration; plan memory, connections and access rules.

overview.label: How billing works
values: Request-based or fixed plans, with storage and transfer limits.
Serverless usage or allocated nodes; engine, storage and transfer affect charges.
Allocated node capacity, replicas and applicable network charges.
Selected tier and capacity; replication and other usage can add charges.

responsibilities.label: Hosted cache service
responsibilities.explanation: The provider operates the cache infrastructure. This comparison covers shared application data caches, not browser or CDN page caching. Managed hosting does not choose which data your app should cache.

responsibilities.label: Expiration and stale data
responsibilities.explanation: An expiration time sets how long a cached value can remain. Your app must set suitable times and refresh or remove stale values when the original data changes. The cache cannot infer your business rules.

responsibilities.label: Sessions and rate limiting
responsibilities.explanation: Sessions can store temporary user state; rate limiting counts requests to enforce a limit. A cache can hold those records, but your app or a connected tool must implement the policy. Neither feature is automatically a complete sign-in service.

responsibilities.label: Access and secrets
responsibilities.explanation: Cache records may contain private data. Keep credentials out of browser code, configure encrypted connections and permitted clients, and separate users' records. A managed service does not enforce your app's user permissions for you.

responsibilities.label: Cache loss and recovery
responsibilities.explanation: Cached values can expire, be evicted when memory fills, or become unavailable. Your app needs a safe fallback and a way to rebuild them. If sessions or counters must survive loss, explicitly check persistence, replication and recovery guarantees for the chosen plan.
